exercises.title: Celsius to Fahrenheit
exercises.statement:
Write celsius_to_fahrenheit(c). It returns the temperature in Fahrenheit.

The formula is F = C × 9 / 5 + 32.
hints: The whole function is one line of arithmetic.
Multiply first, then divide, then add. Python already does * and / before +.
The line starts with return. If your tests print None, the function computed the answer and forgot to hand it back.
exercises.solution:
def celsius_to_fahrenheit(c):
    return c * 9 / 5 + 32
exercises.explanation: Division with / always gives a float, which is why 0 becomes 32.0. The check at −40 is a classic: it is the one temperature where both scales agree.

exercises.title: Even or odd
exercises.statement: Write is_even(n). It returns True when the whole number n is even and False otherwise. Zero and negative even numbers count as even.
hints: Which operator gives the remainder of a division?
n % 2 is 0 for every even number, including 0 and negatives.
A comparison is already a bool. return n % 2 == 0 needs no if.
exercises.solution:
def is_even(n):
    return n % 2 == 0
exercises.explanation: Returning the comparison directly is the habit to build. if x: return True else: return False says the same thing in four lines.

exercises.title: Sum from 1 to n
exercises.statement:
Write sum_to(n). It returns 1 + 2 + ... + n. For n of 0 or less it returns 0.

Use a loop. Do not use the built-in sum.
hints: This is the accumulator pattern: a total that starts at 0 and grows inside a loop.
range(1, n + 1) produces 1 up to and including n. range(1, n) stops one short.
For n of 0 or less the range is empty, the loop body never runs, and the total is still 0. You need no special case.
exercises.explanation: The off-by-one in range is the bug to watch. Notice that the empty range handles zero and negative input for free.

exercises.title: Largest number
exercises.statement:
Write largest(numbers). It returns the largest number in the list, or None for an empty list.

Do not use the built-in max. Walk the list yourself.
hints: Keep the best number seen so far and replace it when a bigger one arrives.
What should 'best so far' be before the loop starts? If you choose 0, a list of negative numbers goes wrong.
Handle the empty list first with if not numbers: return None. Then start from numbers[0].
exercises.explanation: Starting from the first item instead of 0 is the point of the all-negative test. The same pattern finds the best validation loss during training.

exercises.title: FizzBuzz
exercises.statement:
Write fizzbuzz(n). It returns a list of n strings for the numbers 1 to n:

  • multiples of both 3 and 5 become "FizzBuzz"
  • other multiples of 3 become "Fizz"
  • other multiples of 5 become "Buzz"
  • every other number becomes the number as a string
hints: Build a list with a loop and append. Decide what to append with if, elif, else.
Only the first true branch runs. Which test has to come first so that 15 does not become Fizz?
Test i % 15 == 0 first. Turn a number into text with str(i).
exercises.explanation: The order of the branches is the lesson. The most specific case goes first because elif stops at the first match.

exercises.title: Reverse a string
exercises.statement: Write reverse_text(s). It returns the string written backwards.
hints: A slice can take a third number: the step.
A step of -1 walks from the end to the start.
s[::-1]
exercises.solution:
def reverse_text(s):
    return s[::-1]
exercises.explanation: You could also loop and build the string character by character. The slice is the idiom you will see in other people's code.

exercises.title: Count the vowels
exercises.statement: Write count_vowels(s). It returns how many of the characters in s are vowels (a, e, i, o, u). Upper and lower case both count.
hints: Loop over the characters and count the ones you want.
ch in 'aeiou' is True when ch is one of those five letters.
Convert once with s.lower() before the loop so that A and a are treated alike.
exercises.explanation: Normalising the input once, before the loop, is cleaner than testing for ten letters inside it.

exercises.title: Read a text file
exercises.statement:
Write read_text(path). It opens the file at path and returns everything in it as one string.

Read it as UTF-8 so that characters such as é survive.

tests.test:
with open('note.txt', 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    f.write('caf\u00e9 one\ntwo\n')
print(repr(read_text('note.txt')))

hints: Use with open(...) as f: so the file is closed for you.
Pass encoding="utf-8" to open.
f.read() returns the whole file. Return that.
exercises.explanation: On Linux and macOS this often works without the encoding. On Windows it may not. Stating the encoding makes the code behave the same everywhere.

exercises.title: Count characters
exercises.statement:
Write count_chars(text). It returns a dictionary that maps each character to how many times it appears.

Do not use collections.Counter. Build the dictionary yourself.
hints: Start with an empty dictionary and loop over the characters.
The first time you meet a character it is not in the dictionary yet. counts.get(ch, 0) gives 0 in that case.
counts[ch] = counts.get(ch, 0) + 1
exercises.explanation: A space is a character too, which the second test checks. This counting loop comes back, almost unchanged, when you count pairs of tokens.

exercises.title: Most frequent items
exercises.statement:
Write top_n(counts, n). counts is a dictionary of item to count. Return the n most frequent as a list of (item, count) tuples.

  • highest count first
  • when two counts are equal, the smaller item comes first
  • if n is larger than the dictionary, return everything
hints: counts.items() gives the (item, count) pairs. Sort them, then slice.
sorted takes a key function, and a key can return a tuple: first the thing to sort by, then the tie-breaker.
Sort by (-count, item). The minus puts large counts first while items stay ascending. Then take [:n].
exercises.solution:
def top_n(counts, n):
    return sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))[:n]
exercises.explanation: Slicing past the end of a list is not an error in Python, so [:n] handles the case where n is too large. Negating the count is a neat way to mix a descending and an ascending order in one sort.

exercises.title: Split into words
exercises.statement:
Write split_words(text). It returns a list of lower-case words.

  • split on whitespace
  • remove these characters from the start and end of each word: . , ! ? ; : " ' ( )
  • leave characters inside a word alone, so it's stays it's
  • drop anything that ends up empty
hints: Three string methods do all the work: lower, split and strip.
text.split() with no argument splits on any run of spaces, tabs and line breaks.
word.strip(".,!?;:\"'()") removes those characters from both ends only. After stripping, keep the word only if it is not empty.
exercises.explanation: strip with an argument removes any of the listed characters from the ends, not that exact sequence. An empty string is falsy, so if w: drops the leftovers.

exercises.title: Build a vocabulary
exercises.statement:
Write vocabulary(text). It returns a sorted list of the distinct characters in text.

This list is a character-level model's entire alphabet.
hints: Which collection keeps each value only once?
set(text) gives the distinct characters, in no particular order.
sorted(...) turns any collection into a sorted list.
exercises.solution:
def vocabulary(text):
    return sorted(set(text))
exercises.explanation: Sorting matters. Without it the order could differ from run to run, and every token id in your model would change with it.

exercises.title: A character tokenizer
exercises.statement:
Write the class CharTokenizer. It turns text into a list of integers and back, one integer per character.

__init__(self, text) builds the vocabulary and sets four attributes:

  • self.chars: sorted list of the distinct characters in text
  • self.vocab_size: how many there are
  • self.stoi: dictionary from character to its position in self.chars
  • self.itos: dictionary from position to character

encode(self, s) returns the list of integers for s. If s contains a character that is not in the vocabulary, raise ValueError.

decode(self, ids) returns the string for a list of integers.

tests.test:
tok = CharTokenizer('hello world')
print(tok.stoi['h'], tok.itos[3], len(tok.stoi), len(tok.itos))

tok = CharTokenizer('hello world')
print([tok.decode([7, 5, 6, 4, 1]), tok.decode(tok.encode('low hero'))])

hints: __init__ is the vocabulary exercise plus two dictionaries. Store everything on self.
enumerate(self.chars) gives (position, character) pairs, which is what both dictionaries need.
In encode, check if ch not in self.stoi: raise ValueError(...) before looking it up. In decode, look each id up in self.itos and glue the characters together with "".join(...).
exercises.explanation: Real LLM tokenizers use pieces of words instead of single characters, but they expose the same two methods. Raising ValueError yourself gives a clearer message than the KeyError a bare lookup would produce.

exercises.title: Training pairs
exercises.statement:
Write make_pairs(ids). It returns every pair of neighbours as a list of (current, next) tuples.

These pairs are a language model's training examples: after this token came that one.
hints: A list of 4 items has 3 pairs. Which positions start a pair?
Loop i over range(len(ids) - 1) and pair ids[i] with ids[i + 1].
For a list of one item or none the range is empty, so you get [] without a special case.
exercises.solution:
def make_pairs(ids):
    return [(ids[i], ids[i + 1]) for i in range(len(ids) - 1)]
exercises.explanation: zip(ids, ids[1:]) does the same thing in a more Pythonic way. In PyTorch you will build these as two tensors, the inputs and the targets shifted by one.

exercises.title: Train and validation split
exercises.statement:
Write split_data(ids, train_fraction). It cuts ids into two lists and returns them as a pair (train, validation).

The first int(len(ids) * train_fraction) items are the training part. The rest are the validation part.
hints: Work out one number, the cut point, then slice twice.
n = int(len(ids) * train_fraction)
ids[:n] is the first n items and ids[n:] is the rest. Return both, separated by a comma.
exercises.explanation: A model is scored on data it never trained on. If the validation loss is much worse than the training loss, the model has memorised instead of learned.

exercises.title: Count bigrams
exercises.statement:
Write count_bigrams(ids, vocab_size). It returns a grid (a list of lists) of size vocab_size × vocab_size.

counts[a][b] is how many times token b came directly after token a in ids.
hints: Two steps: build a grid of zeros, then walk over the neighbouring pairs and add 1 in the right cell.
If every row of your answer looks the same, you built the grid with [[0] * n] * n. That repeats one row. Build each row separately.
counts = [[0] * vocab_size for _ in range(vocab_size)], then for each i in range(len(ids) - 1) do counts[ids[i]][ids[i + 1]] += 1.
exercises.explanation: This grid is the entire model. Row a holds everything the model knows about what follows token a. A neural language model replaces the grid with a function, but it answers the same question.

exercises.title: Counts to probabilities
exercises.statement:
Write to_probs(row). It turns a row of counts into probabilities that add up to 1 by dividing each count by the row total.

If the total is 0, give every position the same probability.
hints: Work out the total once, then divide every count by it.
Check for a total of 0 before dividing.
With a total of 0, each of the len(row) positions gets 1 / len(row).
exercises.explanation: Turning scores into a distribution that sums to 1 is called normalising. Softmax, which you will write in Stage 1, does the same job for scores that can be negative.

exercises.title: Sample from a distribution
exercises.statement:
Write sample(probs, rng). It picks one index at random, choosing index i with probability probs[i].

rng is a random.Random object. Do not use random.choices. Do it by hand:

  1. take r = rng.random(), a number from 0 up to but not including 1
  2. walk through probs keeping a running total
  3. return the first index where r is less than the running total
  4. if you reach the end without returning, return the last index
hints: Picture the probabilities laid end to end on a line from 0 to 1. r is a dart. Which segment did it hit?
Keep running = 0.0. For each index add its probability, then compare.
The comparison is r < running, not <=. With <=, an index whose probability is 0 could be chosen when r is exactly 0. After the loop, return len(probs) - 1.
exercises.explanation: The fallback on the last line matters because floating-point sums can land a hair under 1. Every text generator ends in this step: turn scores into probabilities, then sample one token.

exercises.title: Generate a sequence
exercises.statement:
Write generate(counts, start_id, length, rng). It returns a list of exactly length token ids.

The first id is start_id. Each following id is sampled from the probabilities of the row that belongs to the id before it.

Paste your own to_probs and sample into this file and use them.

tests.test:
import random
out = generate([[1, 1], [1, 1]], 0, 50, random.Random(1))
print(len(out), sorted(set(out)))

hints: Start a list with start_id in it and grow it until it has length items.
The row to sample from is counts[out[-1]], the row of the most recent token.
while len(out) < length: out.append(sample(to_probs(counts[out[-1]]), rng))
exercises.explanation: This loop is called autoregressive generation: the model's own output becomes its next input. GPT generates text with exactly this loop around a much larger model.

exercises.title: Average loss
exercises.statement:
Write average_loss(counts, ids). It returns how surprised the bigram model is by the sequence ids. Lower is better.

For each neighbouring pair (a, b) in ids, the model's probability is

p = (counts[a][b] + 1) / (sum(counts[a]) + vocab_size)

where vocab_size is the number of rows. The +1 keeps a pair the model never saw from getting probability 0.

The loss for one pair is -math.log(p). Return the average over all pairs.
hints: Walk over the neighbouring pairs, add up -math.log(p) for each, and divide by the number of pairs.
vocab_size is len(counts). The denominator is the row total plus vocab_size.
Check your formula on the second test by hand: with no counts at all, every p is 1 / 5, so the answer is math.log(5).
exercises.solution:
import math


def average_loss(counts, ids):
    vocab_size = len(counts)
    total = 0.0
    pairs = 0
    for i in range(len(ids) - 1):
        a, b = ids[i], ids[i + 1]
        p = (counts[a][b] + 1) / (sum(counts[a]) + vocab_size)
        total += -math.log(p)
        pairs += 1
    return total / pairs
exercises.explanation: This number is the cross-entropy loss, the same quantity used to train GPT. A model that knows nothing scores log(vocab_size), so any trained model should come in below that.

exercises.title: Contains a duplicate
exercises.statement: Write has_duplicate(nums). It returns True if any value appears more than once and False otherwise.
hints: Which collection throws away repeats?
Compare the number of distinct values with the number of values.
len(set(nums)) != len(nums)
exercises.solution:
def has_duplicate(nums):
    return len(set(nums)) != len(nums)
exercises.explanation: A set gives the answer in n steps. A loop that adds to a set and returns as soon as it meets a repeat is just as fast and stops early.

exercises.title: Anagrams
exercises.statement: Write are_anagrams(a, b). It returns True if b uses exactly the same characters as a, the same number of times each, in any order.
hints: Two strings are anagrams when their character counts are the same.
Build a count dictionary for each string and compare the two dictionaries with ==.
A helper counts(s) that loops and does d[ch] = d.get(ch, 0) + 1 keeps it tidy.
exercises.explanation: sorted(a) == sorted(b) also works and is shorter, at the cost of sorting (n log n instead of n). Interviewers often ask for both and the trade-off.

exercises.title: Pair with a given sum
exercises.statement:
Write pair_with_sum(nums, target). Find two different positions i < j whose values add up to target and return them as the tuple (i, j). Return None if there is no such pair.

If several pairs work, return the one whose j is smallest, and for that j the smallest i.

Aim for one pass over the list.
hints: Checking every pair with two loops works but takes n² steps. What could you remember as you walk the list to avoid the inner loop?
When you are at value x, the partner you need is target - x. A dictionary can tell you at once whether you have already seen it, and where.
Keep seen = {} from value to its first position. For each j, x: if target - x is in seen, return (seen[target - x], j). Otherwise store x if it is not there yet.
exercises.explanation: Trading memory for time with a dictionary turns n² steps into n. Checking before storing is what stops one element from pairing with itself. This is the first pattern to reach for whenever a problem says 'find two things that together...'.

exercises.title: The missing number
exercises.statement:
Write missing_number(nums). The list holds n different numbers taken from 0 to n inclusive, so exactly one number in that range is absent. Return it.

Use only a few variables of extra memory.
hints: A set would work, but it uses memory proportional to the list. What do you know about the numbers 0 to n taken together?
The sum of 0 to n is n * (n + 1) // 2. Compare it with the sum of the list.
n = len(nums), then return the expected sum minus sum(nums).
exercises.explanation: The same idea works with XOR in place of addition, which avoids large sums in languages with fixed-size integers. Either way it is one pass and constant memory.

exercises.title: Range sums in constant time
exercises.statement:
Write the class PrefixSums. It is created from a list of numbers that will not change. Its method total(i, j) returns the sum of the values from position i to position j, both included.

total will be called many times, so it must not loop over the range.

tests.test:
p = PrefixSums([-2, 0, 3, -5, 2, -1])
print(p.total(0, 2), p.total(2, 5), p.total(0, 5), p.total(3, 3))

hints: Do the adding once, in __init__, and store running totals.
Let prefix[k] be the sum of the first k values, with prefix[0] = 0. It has one more entry than the list.
The sum from i to j is prefix[j + 1] - prefix[i].
exercises.explanation: Paying n once to answer every later question in constant time is the trade behind prefix sums. The extra leading 0 removes the special case for ranges that start at position 0.

exercises.title: Most frequent values
exercises.statement: Write most_frequent(nums, k). It returns the k values that appear most often, most frequent first. When two values appear equally often, the smaller value comes first.
hints: Two steps: count, then pick the top k.
Sort the distinct values by a key that puts high counts first and breaks ties by the value.
sorted(counts, key=lambda v: (-counts[v], v))[:k]
exercises.explanation: Sorting costs n log n. A heap of size k, or bucketing values by their count, brings that down, and is the usual follow-up question.

exercises.title: Longest run of consecutive numbers
exercises.statement:
Write longest_consecutive(nums). The list is in no particular order. Return the length of the longest run of consecutive whole numbers that can be found among its values. Repeats count once.

For [100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2] the run is 1, 2, 3, 4, so the answer is 4.

Aim for about n steps, without sorting.
hints: Put the values in a set so that 'is x + 1 present?' is instant.
Counting upward from every value repeats work. From which values is it worth starting a count?
Only start at x when x - 1 is not in the set, because then x is the beginning of a run. Count x + 1, x + 2, ... while they are present.
exercises.explanation: The inner while looks like it makes this n², but each value is visited by it at most once, because counting only starts at the beginning of a run. Spotting that is the point of the problem.

exercises.title: Count subarrays with a given sum
exercises.statement: Write count_subarrays(nums, k). It returns how many contiguous, non-empty stretches of nums add up to k. The numbers can be negative.
hints: Let prefix[i] be the sum of the first i numbers. The stretch from i to j adds up to prefix[j] - prefix[i].
So a stretch ending here sums to k exactly when some earlier prefix equals current_prefix - k. Count how many earlier prefixes had each value.
Keep seen = {0: 1}. For each number: add it to the running total, add seen.get(total - k, 0) to the answer, then record the total in seen.
exercises.explanation: Prefix sums plus a dictionary is the pair-with-sum idea applied to running totals. The starting entry {0: 1} stands for the empty prefix, so stretches that begin at position 0 are counted. A sliding window does not work here because negative numbers break it.

exercises.title: Palindrome, ignoring punctuation
exercises.statement: Write is_palindrome(s). Looking only at letters and digits, and treating upper and lower case alike, does s read the same in both directions?

tests.test: print(is_palindrome('A man, a plan, a canal: Panama'), is_palindrome('race a car'))

hints: Put one pointer at each end and walk them toward each other.
ch.isalnum() is True for letters and digits. Skip anything else.
While i < j: move i right past non-alphanumerics, move j left past them, compare s[i].lower() with s[j].lower(), then step both.
exercises.explanation: Two pointers use no extra memory. Cleaning the string first and comparing it with its reverse is shorter and also fine; say which trade-off you chose.

exercises.title: Pair with a given sum in a sorted list
exercises.statement:
Write sorted_pair_sum(nums, target). nums is sorted in ascending order. Return two of its values (a, b), taken from different positions with a <= b, that add up to target. Return None if no pair does.

If several pairs work, return the one with the smallest a.

Use no extra memory beyond a few variables.
hints: Because the list is sorted, the smallest and largest values tell you which way to move.
Start with lo at the first position and hi at the last. If the sum is too small, only moving lo right can help. If it is too large, only moving hi left can.
Loop while lo < hi. Return (nums[lo], nums[hi]) when the sum matches.
exercises.explanation: Each step discards one value for good, so the loop runs at most n times. Compare with the dictionary version: sorted input lets you drop the extra memory.

exercises.title: Move zeros to the end
exercises.statement: Write move_zeros(nums). Return a list with the same values in which every zero has been moved to the end and the other values keep their order.
hints: Collect the non-zero values in order, then add the right number of zeros.
The number of zeros is the original length minus the number of values you kept.
For the in-place version an interviewer may ask for: keep a write position, copy each non-zero value to it, then fill the rest with zeros.
exercises.explanation: The in-place version uses a slow pointer for the next write position and a fast pointer for reading. That read-and-write pair is the second common form of the two-pointer pattern.

exercises.title: Best day to buy and sell
exercises.statement: Write max_profit(prices). prices[i] is the price on day i. You may buy on one day and sell on a later day. Return the largest profit possible, or 0 if no trade makes a profit.
hints: For each day, the best sale is against the lowest price seen on any earlier day.
Walk once, keeping the lowest price so far.
For each price: update the best profit with price - lowest, then update lowest. Start best at 0.
exercises.explanation: Tracking the best candidate so far turns the n² comparison of every pair of days into one pass. The same shape appears in Kadane's algorithm.

exercises.title: Squares of a sorted list
exercises.statement:
Write sorted_squares(nums). nums is sorted in ascending order and may contain negative numbers. Return the squares of its values, in ascending order.

Do it in one pass, without calling a sort.
hints: Squaring breaks the order because of the negatives. Where are the largest squares?
The largest square is always at one of the two ends. Put a pointer at each end.
Fill the answer from the back: compare abs(nums[lo]) with abs(nums[hi]), write the larger square at the current last free position, and move that pointer inward.
exercises.explanation: Sorting the squares would cost n log n. Using the fact that the input is already sorted brings it to n, which is the point an interviewer wants you to notice.

exercises.title: Three numbers that sum to zero
exercises.statement:
Write three_sum(nums). Return every different triple of values from nums, taken from three different positions, that adds up to 0.

Write each triple as a list in ascending order, return each triple once, and return the triples in ascending order.
hints: Sort first. Then fix the smallest of the three and look for the other two in the rest.
With the first value fixed, the rest is 'pair with a given sum in a sorted list', which two pointers solve in one pass.
Skip a first value equal to the previous one, and after recording a triple move lo past equal values, so that no triple is produced twice.
exercises.explanation: Sorting costs n log n and the loop is n², so n² overall, against n³ for three nested loops. Handling duplicates by skipping equal neighbours, instead of with a set, is the part that takes care.

exercises.title: Largest sum of k neighbours
exercises.statement: Write max_window_sum(nums, k). It returns the largest sum of any k consecutive values. Return None if k is less than 1 or larger than the list.
hints: Adding up every window from scratch repeats almost all of the work.
When the window slides one step, one value enters and one leaves.
Start with sum(nums[:k]). For each i from k on: window += nums[i] - nums[i - k], and keep the best.
exercises.explanation: Updating the sum instead of recomputing it turns n × k steps into n. Start best from the first window, not from 0, or an all-negative list gives the wrong answer.

exercises.title: Longest stretch without a repeated character
exercises.statement: Write longest_unique(s). It returns the length of the longest stretch of consecutive characters in s in which no character appears twice.
hints: Keep a window [start, i] that never contains a repeat. Grow it on the right, and shrink it from the left only when you must.
Remember the last position of each character. When the new character was last seen inside the window, move start to just after that position.
start = max(start, last[ch] + 1). The max matters: the test 'abba' fails without it, because the old a lies before the window.
exercises.explanation: A sliding window works when making the window longer can only break the condition and making it shorter can only repair it. Both ends only ever move right, so the whole thing is n steps.

exercises.title: Shortest stretch reaching a total
exercises.statement: Write min_subarray_len(target, nums). All numbers are positive. Return the length of the shortest contiguous stretch whose sum is at least target, or 0 if there is none.
hints: Because every number is positive, a longer window always has a larger sum. That is what makes a sliding window valid here.
Grow the window on the right. Whenever the sum is large enough, record the length and shrink from the left.
For each right end: add the value; while total >= target: update the best length, subtract nums[left], and move left up.
exercises.explanation: Each element enters the window once and leaves at most once, so the nested loop is still n steps. With negative numbers this breaks, and you would need prefix sums instead.

exercises.title: Balanced brackets
exercises.statement: Write balanced(s). It returns True if every (, [ and { in s is closed by the matching bracket in the right order. Other characters are ignored.
hints: The most recently opened bracket must be the first one closed. Which data structure is last in, first out?
Push every opening bracket onto a list. On a closing bracket, the top of the list must be its partner.
A dictionary {')': '(', ']': '[', '}': '{'} tells you the partner. Fail if the stack is empty or the top does not match. At the end the stack must be empty.
exercises.explanation: Two easy mistakes: popping from an empty stack on input like ], and forgetting that leftovers such as (( are unbalanced. A Python list with append and pop is the stack.

exercises.title: Evaluate reverse Polish notation
exercises.statement:
Write eval_rpn(tokens). tokens is a list of strings: whole numbers and the operators +, -, *, /. In reverse Polish notation an operator comes after its two operands, so ['2', '1', '+', '3', '*'] means (2 + 1) × 3.

Return the result as an int. Division drops the fractional part, rounding toward zero, so 7 / −2 is −3.
hints: Numbers wait on a stack until an operator arrives to use the top two.
The first value you pop is the right-hand operand. Getting that backwards breaks - and /.
Python's // rounds down, so 7 // -2 is −4. Divide the absolute values with // and put the sign back afterwards.
exercises.explanation: The check t in ('+', '-', '*', '/') has to come before int(t), and it must not mistake '-2' for an operator, which is why it compares whole tokens. Rounding toward zero is the detail interviewers look for.

exercises.title: A stack that knows its minimum
exercises.statement:
Write the class MinStack with four methods, each taking constant time:

  • push(x) adds x on top
  • pop() removes the top value
  • top() returns the top value
  • get_min() returns the smallest value currently in the stack

tests.test:
s = MinStack()
s.push(-2)
s.push(0)
s.push(-3)
print(s.get_min())
s.pop()
print(s.top(), s.get_min())

s = MinStack()
s.push(1)
s.push(1)
s.pop()
print(s.get_min(), s.top())
s.push(5)
s.push(0)
s.pop()
print(s.get_min())

hints: Scanning for the minimum takes n steps. What could each entry remember so that no scan is needed?
Store, with every value, the minimum of everything at or below it.
Push the pair (x, min(x, current_min)). get_min is then the second part of the top pair, and popping restores the previous minimum for free.
exercises.explanation: Keeping a second piece of information beside each entry is a common way to make a query constant-time. A separate stack of minimums does the same job with a little less memory.

exercises.title: A queue made of two stacks
exercises.statement:
Write the class Queue, using two Python lists that you only ever append to and pop() from the end of.

  • put(x) adds x at the back
  • get() removes and returns the value at the front, and raises IndexError if the queue is empty
  • size() returns how many values are waiting

tests.test:
q = Queue()
q.put(1)
q.put(2)
print(q.get())
q.put(3)
print(q.get(), q.get(), q.size())

hints: Pouring one stack into another reverses its order. Reversing a stack gives you the oldest item on top.
Keep an inbox for put and an outbox for get. Only when the outbox is empty, pour the whole inbox into it.
In get: if outbox is empty, while self.inbox: self.outbox.append(self.inbox.pop()). Then pop from outbox, which raises IndexError by itself if both are empty.
exercises.explanation: Each value is moved between the stacks at most once, so although one get can be slow, the average cost per operation is constant. That argument is called amortised analysis. In real Python code use collections.deque.

exercises.title: Next greater value
exercises.statement: Write next_greater(nums). Return a list of the same length in which position i holds the first value to the right of nums[i] that is larger than it, or -1 if there is none.
hints: The two-loop answer is n². Think of the values still waiting for their answer as you walk left to right.
Keep a stack of positions that have no answer yet. When a new value arrives, it is the answer for every waiting position with a smaller value.
For each i: while the stack is not empty and nums[stack[-1]] < nums[i], pop a position and set its answer to nums[i]. Then push i.
exercises.explanation: This is a monotonic stack: the waiting values always decrease from bottom to top. Each position is pushed once and popped at most once, so it is n steps overall.

exercises.title: Binary search
exercises.statement:
Write binary_search(nums, target). nums is sorted in ascending order with no repeats. Return the position of target, or -1 if it is not there.

Do not scan the whole list. Halve the search range at every step.
hints: Keep two positions, lo and hi, that bracket where the target could be.
Look at the middle. If it is too small, the target can only be to the right, so move lo to mid + 1. If too large, move hi to mid - 1.
Loop while lo <= hi. With < instead of <= you never look at the last remaining element.
exercises.explanation: Each step halves the range, so a million items need about twenty looks. Decide once whether hi is inside the range or just past it and stay consistent; most binary search bugs come from mixing the two.

exercises.title: First position at least x
exercises.statement: Write first_at_least(nums, x). nums is sorted in ascending order and may contain repeats. Return the smallest position i with nums[i] >= x. If every value is smaller than x, return len(nums).
hints: You are not looking for a value. You are looking for the boundary between 'too small' and 'big enough'.
Let the answer range be lo to hi with hi starting at len(nums), because that is a legal answer.
While lo < hi: if nums[mid] < x, the answer is to the right, so lo = mid + 1. Otherwise mid might be the answer, so hi = mid. Return lo.
exercises.explanation: This is the lower-bound form, the most reusable version of binary search. Any question that can be phrased as 'find the first position where a condition becomes true' is this loop with a different test.

exercises.title: Whole-number square root
exercises.statement:
Write int_sqrt(n) for a whole number n of 0 or more. Return the largest whole number r with r * r <= n.

Do not use math.sqrt or ** 0.5. It must stay exact for very large n.
hints: There is no list here, but there is a range of possible answers, 0 to n, and a test that is true up to some point and false after it.
Binary search on the answer: is mid * mid <= n?
You want the last value that passes. Use mid = (lo + hi + 1) // 2, and on a pass set lo = mid, otherwise hi = mid - 1. Rounding the middle up stops the loop from getting stuck.
exercises.explanation: Searching over answers instead of over a list is the idea behind a whole family of interview problems: smallest capacity, fewest days, largest minimum distance. If you can test a candidate answer and the test flips only once, you can binary search it.

exercises.title: The number that appears once
exercises.statement:
Write single_number(nums). Every value appears exactly twice, except one that appears once. Return that one.

Use one pass and no extra collection.
hints: There is an operator for which a ? a is 0 and a ? 0 is a.
That operator is XOR, written ^. Order does not matter for it.
XOR every number into one variable that starts at 0. The pairs cancel and the single value is left.
exercises.explanation: XOR is its own inverse, so every pair cancels wherever its two members sit in the list. A dictionary of counts also works but uses memory proportional to the input.

exercises.title: Count the one-bits
exercises.statement:
Write count_bits(n). Return a list of length n + 1 in which position i holds the number of 1s in the binary form of i.

Do not convert numbers to strings. Reuse earlier answers so that each entry takes constant time.
hints: Compare the bits of i with the bits of i // 2.
i >> 1 is i with its last bit removed, and i & 1 is that last bit.
out[i] = out[i >> 1] + (i & 1), filled in from 1 upward.
exercises.explanation: This is dynamic programming on the binary form: the answer for a number is built from the answer for a smaller one that is already known.

exercises.title: Merge sort
exercises.statement:
Write merge_sort(nums). It returns a new list with the same values in ascending order.

Do not use sorted or .sort(). Split the list in half, sort each half the same way, and merge the two sorted halves.
hints: A recursive function needs a case it can answer without calling itself. A list of 0 or 1 items is already sorted.
Split at len(nums) // 2, call merge_sort on each half, then merge.
To merge: keep one position in each half, repeatedly take the smaller of the two front values, and when one half runs out append the rest of the other.
exercises.explanation: The list is halved about log n times and each level does n work in merging, so the total is n log n. Using <= when the two front values are equal keeps equal items in their original order, which makes the sort stable.

exercises.title: Quicksort
exercises.statement:
Write quick_sort(nums). It returns a new list with the same values in ascending order.

Do not use sorted or .sort(). Pick one value as the pivot, split the rest into the values smaller than the pivot, equal to it, and larger than it, sort the smaller and the larger groups the same way, and join the three.

tests.test:
data = [(i * 7919) % 1009 for i in range(1500)]
out = quick_sort(data)
print(out[:5], out[-3:], len(out), out == sorted(data), quick_sort(list(range(600)))[-1])

hints: A list of 0 or 1 values is already sorted. That is the case that stops the recursion.
Use the middle value as the pivot: pivot = nums[len(nums) // 2]. Three list comprehensions build the three groups.
return quick_sort(smaller) + equal + quick_sort(larger). Keeping the equal values out of both recursive calls is what makes a list of repeats finish at once.
exercises.explanation: When the pivot splits the list roughly in half the cost follows T(n) = 2 T(n/2) + n, which the master theorem solves as n log n, the same recurrence as merge sort. When the pivot is always the smallest value it becomes T(n) = T(n − 1) + n, which is n². Taking the first element as pivot makes a sorted input the worst case, which is why this version takes the middle and library versions take a random one or the median of three. The in-place version, which partitions by swapping inside one array, uses no extra lists and is the one meant when quicksort is called fast.

exercises.title: All subsets
exercises.statement: Write all_subsets(items). items is a list of distinct values. Return a list containing every subset, each as a list that keeps the values in their original order. The subsets can come in any order, and the empty subset is included.
hints: Every value is either in a subset or not. That is two choices per value, so n values give 2ⁿ subsets.
Suppose you already have every subset of the first few values. Adding one more value doubles the collection: each old subset, and each old subset with the new value on the end.
Start with out = [[]]. For each value x: out = out + [s + [x] for s in out].
exercises.explanation: The recursive version makes the same choice explicitly: at each position, branch once without the value and once with it. That include-or-skip recursion is the template for combination sum, permutations and most backtracking problems.

exercises.title: All orderings
exercises.statement:
Write permutations(items). items is a list of distinct values. Return a list of every ordering of them, each as a list. The orderings can come in any order. For an empty list, return one empty ordering.

Do not use itertools.
hints: Choose the first element. What is left to solve is the same problem on a shorter list.
For each position i: take items[i] as the first element and put it in front of every ordering of the rest.
The rest is items[:i] + items[i + 1:]. The base case is the empty list, which has exactly one ordering: [[]].
exercises.explanation: There are n! orderings, so no algorithm can be faster than that. The backtracking form, which swaps elements in place and undoes the swap after each recursive call, avoids building the rest lists.

exercises.title: Reverse a linked list
exercises.statement:
A linked list is a chain of Node objects. Each node has a value and a next that points to the following node, or is None at the end.

Write reverse_list(head). Given the first node, reverse the chain and return the new first node. For an empty list (None) return None.

Leave the Node class as it is.
hints: Walk along the chain and turn each arrow around so that it points at the node before.
Once you change node.next you have lost the way forward, so save the following node first.
Keep prev = None. While head: nxt = head.next, head.next = prev, prev = head, head = nxt. Return prev.
exercises.explanation: Draw three boxes and the arrows on paper and move them by hand once; the order of the four lines then stops being something to memorise. It runs in n steps and uses no extra memory.

exercises.title: Middle of a linked list
exercises.statement:
Write middle_value(head). Return the value stored in the middle node of the linked list. If the list has an even number of nodes, use the second of the two middle nodes. For an empty list return None.

Go through the list only once.
hints: Counting the nodes and then walking half way is two passes. Can two pointers do it in one?
Move one pointer one step at a time and another two steps at a time.
while fast and fast.next: advance slow by one and fast by two. When the loop ends, slow is at the middle.
exercises.explanation: The fast pointer reaches the end when the slow one is half way. This slow-and-fast pair is the standard tool for linked lists and comes back in cycle detection.

exercises.title: Does the list loop?
exercises.statement:
Write has_cycle(head). Following next from head either reaches None or goes round a loop forever. Return True if there is a loop.

Use constant extra memory.

tests.test:
a, b, c, d = Node(1), Node(2), Node(3), Node(4)
a.next, b.next, c.next, d.next = b, c, d, b
print(has_cycle(a))

a, b, c = Node(1), Node(2), Node(3)
a.next, b.next = b, c
s = Node(9)
s.next = s
print(has_cycle(a), has_cycle(None), has_cycle(s), has_cycle(Node(5)))

hints: A set of visited nodes works but uses memory. Think of two runners on a track.
If there is a loop, a runner moving two steps at a time must eventually catch one moving one step at a time.
Advance slow by one and fast by two while fast and fast.next. Return True if they ever are the same node (is), and False when the loop ends.
exercises.explanation: This is Floyd's cycle detection. Compare nodes with is, not ==: two different nodes can hold equal values.

exercises.title: Merge two sorted lists
exercises.statement: Write merge_sorted(a, b). a and b are the first nodes of two linked lists, each sorted in ascending order (either may be None). Join the nodes into one sorted list and return its first node.
hints: It is the merge step of merge sort, on nodes instead of list positions.
A dummy first node saves you from treating the first real node as a special case.
Keep tail at the end of the result. Attach the smaller of a and b, advance that one, advance tail. When one list runs out, attach the rest of the other. Return dummy.next.
exercises.explanation: The dummy node is the trick to remember: it gives tail something to stand on before the first real node is chosen.

exercises.title: Ways to climb stairs
exercises.statement: Write count_ways(n). You climb n steps, taking 1 or 2 steps at a time. Return the number of different sequences of moves that reach the top exactly. For n of 0 the answer is 1 (do nothing).
hints: Think about the last move. It was either a single step or a double.
So ways(n) = ways(n - 1) + ways(n - 2). Plain recursion on that recomputes the same values again and again and is far too slow for 30.
Build upward instead, keeping only the last two answers: a, b = 1, 1, then repeat a, b = b, a + b.
exercises.explanation: Defining the answer in terms of smaller answers and then computing each smaller answer once is all that dynamic programming means. The plain recursive version takes roughly 2ⁿ calls; this one takes n steps.

exercises.title: Largest sum of a stretch
exercises.statement: Write max_subarray(nums) for a non-empty list. Return the largest sum that any contiguous, non-empty stretch of it can have. The numbers can be negative.
hints: Ask a smaller question: what is the best stretch that ends exactly here?
The best stretch ending here is either this number alone or this number added to the best stretch ending just before it.
current = max(x, current + x), and best = max(best, current). Start both from the first number so that an all-negative list works.
exercises.explanation: This is Kadane's algorithm, and it is dynamic programming in its smallest form: the answer for each position is built from the answer for the one before it, and only that one value needs to be kept.

exercises.title: Fewest coins
exercises.statement: Write min_coins(coins, amount). coins lists the coin values you may use, each as many times as you like. Return the smallest number of coins that add up to exactly amount, or -1 if it cannot be done.
hints: Always taking the largest coin fails: with coins 1, 3, 4 and amount 6 it gives 4 + 1 + 1, but 3 + 3 is better.
Let best[a] be the fewest coins for amount a. The last coin used was some c, which leaves a - c.
best[0] = 0. For each a from 1 to amount, best[a] is 1 plus the smallest best[a - c] over coins c <= a that can be made. Use a large number for 'cannot be made'.
exercises.explanation: The table is filled from small amounts to large, so every value it needs is already there. Using amount + 1 as the 'impossible' marker works because no answer can need more than amount coins.

exercises.title: Depth of a binary tree
exercises.statement:
A binary tree is made of TreeNode objects. Each has a value, a left child and a right child; a missing child is None.

Write max_depth(root). Return the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to a leaf. An empty tree has depth 0.
hints: A tree is a node plus two smaller trees. Most tree answers are built from the answers for those two.
The depth of a tree is 1 for the root plus the larger of the depths of its two subtrees.
if root is None: return 0, otherwise return 1 + max(max_depth(root.left), max_depth(root.right)).
exercises.explanation: This three-line shape, a base case for the empty tree and a combination of the two recursive answers, solves a large share of tree questions. Learn to write it without thinking.

exercises.title: Mirror a binary tree
exercises.statement: Write invert(root). Swap the left and right child of every node in the tree, and return the root.
hints: Do the job at one node, and let recursion do it everywhere else.
At a node: swap its two children, then invert each child.
root.left, root.right = invert(root.right), invert(root.left), after handling None.
exercises.explanation: Python evaluates the whole right-hand side before assigning, which is why the swap can be written in one line without a temporary variable.

exercises.title: A tree, level by level
exercises.statement: Write level_order(root). Return the values of the tree as a list of lists: the first inner list holds the root, the next holds its children from left to right, and so on. For an empty tree return [].
hints: Recursion goes deep first. Here you want to go wide first.
Keep a list of the nodes on the current level. From it, build the list of nodes on the next level.
While the current level is not empty: record its values, then replace it with every non-None child, left before right.
exercises.explanation: This is breadth-first search. Processing a whole level at a time is the usual way to answer any question that mentions levels, such as averages per level or the rightmost node on each.

exercises.title: Longest path in a tree
exercises.statement: Write diameter(root). Return the number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes of the tree. The path does not have to pass through the root. An empty tree, or a single node, has diameter 0.
hints: The longest path that bends at a given node goes down its left side and down its right side.
So at each node the candidate is height(left) + height(right), measured in nodes. You need the heights anyway.
Write an inner function that returns a subtree's height and, as a side effect, updates the best candidate seen. Use nonlocal or a one-element list for the best value.
exercises.explanation: The function returns one thing (height) and records another (the best path). Computing both in a single pass, instead of calling a separate height function at every node, keeps it at n steps.

exercises.title: Insert into and search a binary search tree
exercises.statement:
In a binary search tree, every value in a node's left subtree is smaller than the node's value, and every value in its right subtree is larger.

Write two functions:

  • bst_insert(root, value) adds value as a new leaf in the right place and returns the root. If the value is already there, the tree is unchanged. Inserting into an empty tree (None) returns a new node.
  • bst_contains(root, value) returns True if the value is in the tree.
hints: At every node one comparison tells you which side to go to. You never need to look at the other side.
For insert: if the tree is empty, the new node is the tree. Otherwise insert into the left or right subtree and attach the result.
root.left = bst_insert(root.left, value) when the value is smaller, the mirror image when larger, and return root in every case.
exercises.explanation: Both operations follow one path from the root, so they cost the height of the tree: about log n when the tree is balanced and n when values were inserted in sorted order.

exercises.title: Is it a binary search tree?
exercises.statement: Write is_valid_bst(root). Return True if the tree is a binary search tree: for every node, all values in its left subtree are strictly smaller and all values in its right subtree are strictly larger. An empty tree is valid.
hints: Checking each node against its two children is not enough. A value deep in the right subtree can still be smaller than the root.
Every node has an allowed range that it inherits from its ancestors. Going left lowers the upper limit, going right raises the lower limit.
Write a helper ok(node, low, high) with None meaning no limit. Fail if the value is outside the range, otherwise check ok(node.left, low, node.value) and ok(node.right, node.value, high).
exercises.explanation: The third test is the trap: 3 sits correctly below 6 but wrongly to the right of 5. Passing limits down the tree is the fix. An in-order walk that checks the values come out strictly increasing is an equally good answer.

exercises.title: The k-th smallest value in a search tree
exercises.statement: Write kth_smallest(root, k). root is a binary search tree with at least k nodes. Return its k-th smallest value, counting from 1.
hints: In which order does a walk that visits left subtree, node, right subtree meet the values of a search tree?
An in-order walk meets them in ascending order. The answer is the k-th value it meets.
Do the walk with an explicit stack so that you can stop early: go left as far as possible pushing nodes, pop one, count it, then move to its right child.
exercises.explanation: Collecting every value into a list and indexing it also works, but walks the whole tree. The stack version stops after k values, which matters when the tree is large and k is small.

exercises.title: The k-th largest value
exercises.statement:
Write kth_largest(nums, k). Return the k-th largest value in the list, counting repeats, so the 2nd largest of [5, 5, 4] is 5.

Do not sort the whole list. Use the heapq module and keep the heap no larger than k.
hints: heapq gives a min-heap: the smallest item is always at position 0 and can be removed quickly.
Keep a heap of the k largest values seen so far. Its smallest member is then the k-th largest.
Push each value. If the heap grows beyond k, pop the smallest. At the end return heap[0].
exercises.explanation: Sorting costs n log n. The size-k heap costs n log k and needs only k items of memory, which is the answer expected when the data is a stream too large to hold.

exercises.title: The k closest points
exercises.statement: Write k_closest(points, k). Each point is a list [x, y]. Return the k points nearest to the origin (0, 0), nearest first. If two points are equally near, the smaller point (comparing x, then y) comes first.
hints: You only compare distances, so the square root is unnecessary: compare x * x + y * y.
heapq.nsmallest(k, items, key=...) returns the k smallest items by a key, already in order.
Use the key (x * x + y * y, x, y) so that ties are broken the way the question asks.
exercises.explanation: Leaving out the square root is the first thing to say out loud: it is slower and can introduce rounding, and it never changes the order. Be ready to write the size-k heap by hand if asked not to use nsmallest.

exercises.title: Count the islands
exercises.statement: Write count_islands(grid). grid is a list of rows of 0s and 1s, where 1 is land and 0 is water. An island is a group of land cells connected up, down, left or right. Diagonals do not connect. Return the number of islands.
hints: Scan every cell. Each time you find land you have not visited, you have found a new island.
When you find new land, visit everything connected to it before moving on, so that the rest of that island is not counted again.
Keep a seen set of (row, col). From a new land cell, use a list as a stack: pop a cell, and push its four neighbours that are inside the grid, are land, and are not in seen.
exercises.explanation: A grid is a graph whose nodes are cells and whose edges join neighbours. Using a stack makes this depth-first search; a queue would make it breadth-first, and either counts the islands. Marking a cell as seen when you push it, not when you pop it, keeps it from being pushed twice.

exercises.title: Fewest steps between two nodes
exercises.statement: Write shortest_path(graph, start, goal). graph is a dictionary from each node to the list of nodes it is directly connected to. Return the smallest number of connections you must follow to get from start to goal. Return 0 if they are the same node and -1 if goal cannot be reached.
hints: Explore in rings: first everything one step away, then two steps, and so on. The first time you meet the goal, you have the shortest distance.
That is breadth-first search. Use collections.deque as the queue and a set of visited nodes.
Queue (node, distance) pairs starting with (start, 0). Pop from the left, and for each unvisited neighbour mark it visited and push it with distance + 1.
exercises.explanation: Breadth-first search finds shortest paths when every step costs the same. Depth-first search would find a path, but not necessarily the shortest. Popping from the front of a list is slow, which is why a deque is used.

exercises.title: Can every course be taken?
exercises.statement: Write can_finish(n, prerequisites). There are n courses numbered 0 to n - 1. Each pair [a, b] in prerequisites means course b must be taken before course a. Return True if it is possible to take every course.
hints: It is impossible exactly when the requirements go round in a circle. So this is cycle detection in a directed graph.
Count, for each course, how many requirements it still has. A course with none can be taken now.
Take every course with a count of 0, and for each course that depended on it lower the count by 1, adding it to the list when it reaches 0. If you end up having taken all n, there was no cycle.
exercises.solution:
from collections import deque


def can_finish(n, prerequisites):
    needed = [0] * n
    unlocks = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for a, b in prerequisites:
        needed[a] += 1
        unlocks[b].append(a)
    ready = deque(i for i in range(n) if needed[i] == 0)
    taken = 0
    while ready:
        course = ready.popleft()
        taken += 1
        for nxt in unlocks[course]:
            needed[nxt] -= 1
            if needed[nxt] == 0:
                ready.append(nxt)
    return taken == n
exercises.explanation: This is Kahn's algorithm for topological sorting. Courses stuck in a cycle never reach a count of 0, so they are never taken. Build systems and task schedulers use the same idea to order work.

exercises.title: Cheapest route with limited stops
exercises.statement: Write cheapest_flight(n, flights, src, dst, k). There are n cities numbered from 0. Each flight is [from, to, price] and goes one way. Return the lowest total price to travel from src to dst with at most k stops in between, or -1 if that cannot be done.
exercises.starter:
def cheapest_flight(n, flights, src, dst, k):
    pass
hints: At most k stops means at most k + 1 flights. Think about the cheapest price to each city using a limited number of flights.
Let cost[c] be the cheapest price to city c using at most r flights. One more round lets every flight extend a route by one.

Repeat k + 1 times: copy cost to new, and for each flight whose origin is reachable set new[to] = min(new[to], cost[from] + price). Reading from the old list and writing to the copy is what keeps a round to one extra flight.
exercises.explanation: This is the Bellman-Ford algorithm cut off after k + 1 rounds. Updating a copy is the detail that matters: updating in place would let a route gain several flights in one round and break the stop limit.

exercises.title: Minimum spanning tree
exercises.statement:
A network has n nodes, numbered 0 to n - 1, and a list of possible cables. Each cable is (u, v, cost) and joins nodes u and v in both directions.

Write mst_cost(n, edges). Return the smallest total cost of a set of cables that connects every node to every other, directly or through other nodes. Return None if the cables cannot connect all the nodes.

Use Kruskal's method: go through the cables from cheapest to most expensive and take a cable only if its two ends are not connected yet.
hints: The hard part is asking quickly whether two nodes are already connected. Give every node a parent; a group is known by the root you reach by following parents.
find(x): follow parent[x] until a node is its own parent. To join two groups, make one root the parent of the other.
Sort the edges by cost. For each: if find(u) != find(v), join them, add the cost, count one more edge. At the end the tree is complete only if it has n - 1 edges.
exercises.explanation: Taking the cheapest cable that joins two separate groups is always safe: this is the cut property, and it is why a greedy method gives the best answer here. Sorting costs E log E and dominates. The parent structure is called union-find or disjoint sets; the line parent[x] = parent[parent[x]] shortens the path on every lookup, which keeps each find close to constant time. Prim's method reaches the same tree by growing it from one node with a heap, as Dijkstra's algorithm does.

exercises.title: Shortest paths between every pair
exercises.statement:
A road map has n towns, numbered 0 to n - 1, and one-way roads (u, v, length) from u to v.

Write all_pairs(n, roads). Return a matrix as a list of rows: entry [i][j] is the length of the shortest route from i to j, 0 when i equals j, and None when there is no route. Lengths are never negative. If two roads join the same pair of towns, the shorter one counts.

Use the Floyd-Warshall method: allow routes through town 0, then also through town 1, and so on. A route from i to j improves if going by way of the newly allowed town k is shorter.
hints: Start with a matrix of float('inf'), zeros on the diagonal, and each road's length filled in. Turn inf into None at the very end.
Three nested loops, and the order matters: k outside, then i, then j.
if dist[i][k] + dist[k][j] < dist[i][j]: dist[i][j] = dist[i][k] + dist[k][j].
exercises.explanation: This is dynamic programming over the set of towns a route may pass through, and it costs n³ whatever the number of roads. Running Dijkstra's algorithm from every town costs about n · E log n, which wins on a sparse map; Floyd-Warshall wins on a dense one and is three lines long. With k as the innermost loop the method would be wrong: a route would be improved through towns whose own shortest routes are not settled yet. The two inner loops for a fixed k are independent, so they are the part a GPU or an OpenMP parallel for can share out.

exercises.title: Storing a sparse matrix
exercises.statement:
A matrix that is mostly zeros wastes memory as a list of rows. Compressed sparse row form, CSR, stores only the non-zero entries, in three lists:

  • values: the non-zero entries, row by row, left to right
  • cols: the column of each of those entries
  • row_ptr: one entry per row plus one. row_ptr[r] is where row r starts in values, and row_ptr[r + 1] is where it ends

Write to_csr(dense). dense is a list of rows. Return (values, cols, row_ptr).
hints: row_ptr starts as [0]. After finishing each row, append the number of values stored so far.
Walk each row with its column numbers: for c, v in enumerate(row):.
When v != 0: append v to values and c to cols. After the row: row_ptr.append(len(values)).
exercises.explanation: An empty row shows up as two equal neighbours in row_ptr. A million by million matrix with five entries per row takes 5 million values in this form instead of 10¹² numbers. CSR is what scipy.sparse.csr_matrix and the sparse tensors of PyTorch hold, and a pruned neural network is stored this way on an edge device.

exercises.title: Multiplying with a sparse matrix
exercises.statement:
A matrix is given in CSR form: values are its non-zero entries row by row, cols[k] is the column of values[k], and row r owns the entries from row_ptr[r] up to, but not including, row_ptr[r + 1].

Write csr_matvec(values, cols, row_ptr, x). It returns the product of the matrix with the vector x, as a list with one entry per row. Do not rebuild the dense matrix.

    pass

exercises.explanation: The work is proportional to the number of non-zero entries, not to rows times columns. Every iterative solver, Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel included, spends its time in this product. The rows are independent, so the outer loop is an easy parallel for; the catch on a GPU is x[cols[k]], a read from a scattered address, which is the cache lesson once more.

exercises.title: A circulant matrix without the matrix
exercises.statement:
A circulant matrix is fixed by its first row c. Every row is the row above shifted one place to the right, with the last entry wrapping round to the front. So the entry in row i, column j is c[(j - i) % n].

Write circulant_matvec(c, x). It returns the product of that matrix with the vector x, without storing the matrix: n numbers describe it completely.
hints: Row i of the product is the sum over j of (the entry at row i, column j) times x[j].
That entry is c[(j - i) % n]. In Python % already returns a result from 0 to n - 1 for a negative left side.
[sum(c[(j - i) % n] * x[j] for j in range(n)) for i in range(n)].
exercises.explanation: The second test shows what such a matrix does: with c = [0, 1, 0, 0] it rotates the vector. Any circulant matrix is a weighted sum of rotations, and multiplying by it is a circular convolution, the operation a convolutional layer performs with wrap-around padding. That is also why the fast Fourier transform diagonalises every circulant matrix and can do this product in n log n steps instead of n². A Toeplitz matrix is the same idea without the wrap-around: constant along each diagonal, and fixed by its first row and first column.

exercises.title: Amdahl's law
exercises.statement:
A fraction f of a program's work can be shared out perfectly among processors. The rest runs on one processor however many there are.

Write three functions.

  • amdahl(f, p) returns the speedup on p processors: 1 / ((1 - f) + f / p).
  • amdahl_limit(f) returns the speedup that no number of processors can pass: 1 / (1 - f). When f is 1 there is no limit, so return float('inf').
  • efficiency(f, p) returns the speedup divided by p: how much of each processor is doing useful work.
hints: Write the time on p processors as a fraction of the time on one: the serial part stays 1 - f, the parallel part becomes f / p.
Speedup is old time over new time, so 1 / ((1 - f) + f / p). For the limit, let p grow until f / p vanishes.
amdahl_limit: if f == 1: return float('inf'), otherwise 1 / (1 - f). efficiency is amdahl(f, p) / p.
exercises.explanation: With 90% of the work parallel, ten processors give a speedup of 5.3, and a thousand could not give 10. The serial tenth sets the ceiling. Efficiency shows the same thing from the other side: at 100 processors and 99% parallel work, half of every processor is wasted. Gustafson's answer is that people use more processors to solve bigger problems, where the parallel part grows and the serial part does not.

exercises.title: Sharing a loop among threads
exercises.statement:
A loop has n iterations, numbered from 0, and p threads share them. Each thread takes one unbroken run of iterations, in thread order, and the runs are as equal as they can be: when n is not a multiple of p, the first n % p threads take one extra.

Write block_range(n, p, k). It returns (start, end) for thread k: the thread runs iterations start up to, but not including, end.

tests.test: print([block_range(10, 3, k) for k in range(3)])
print([block_range(8, 4, k) for k in range(4)], [block_range(3, 5, k) for k in range(5)])

hints: Every thread gets at least n // p iterations. How many are left over, and who gets them?
Thread k starts after all the threads before it. Each of those took n // p, and the first n % p of them took one more.
q, r = divmod(n, p). start = k * q + min(k, r). end = start + q + (1 if k < r else 0).
exercises.explanation: This is what OpenMP's static schedule does with a for loop, and what an MPI program does by hand when it gives each process its slice of an array. min(k, r) counts how many of the earlier threads took an extra iteration. The formula needs no loop, so every process can work out its own slice without being told.

exercises.title: A direct-mapped cache
exercises.statement:
A cache has lines lines. Each line holds one block of block_size bytes of memory.

  • The byte at address a belongs to block number a // block_size.
  • A block can live in only one line: line number block % lines.
  • Reading an address is a hit if its block is already in its line. Otherwise it is a miss, and the block replaces whatever that line held.

Write cache_misses(addresses, lines, block_size). The cache starts empty. Return the number of misses for the addresses read in the order given.
hints: Keep a list with one entry per line that remembers which block the line holds. None means empty.
For each address work out the block, then the line. Compare the block with what the line holds.
block = a // block_size, line = block % lines. If held[line] != block: count a miss and store block in held[line].
exercises.explanation: Reading memory in order costs one miss per block, because the neighbours arrive with the first byte. That is spatial locality. The second test shows the weakness of direct mapping: addresses 0 and 64 fight over one line and every read misses, although three lines stand empty. Real caches soften this by letting a block choose among a few lines, which is called set-associative.

exercises.title: Row order against column order
exercises.statement:
A matrix of rows by cols numbers is stored row after row from address 0. Each number takes 8 bytes, so the element in row r and column c is at address (r * cols + c) * 8.

Write traversal_misses(rows, cols, order, lines, block_size). It returns the number of cache misses when every element is read once through a direct-mapped cache with lines lines of block_size bytes, starting empty.

  • When order is "row", read row 0 from left to right, then row 1, and so on.
  • When order is "col", read column 0 from top to bottom, then column 1, and so on.

The cache works as in the exercise before: block a // block_size lives in line block % lines.
exercises.starter:
def traversal_misses(rows, cols, order, lines, block_size):
    pass
hints: Two steps: produce the addresses in the order they are read, then count the misses as you did before.
The two orders differ only in which loop is outside. For "col" the column loop is outside and the row loop is inside.
Build addresses with two nested loops and (r * cols + c) * 8, then run the cache: held = [None] * lines, a miss when held[block % lines] != block.
exercises.explanation: For a 64 by 64 matrix the row walk misses 512 times, once per block. The column walk misses on all 4096 reads, because each step jumps a whole row ahead and lands in a different block. Same data, same number of reads, eight times the misses. The middle test shows when the order stops mattering: when the cache can hold the whole matrix. This is why the loop order of a matrix product matters, and why NumPy asks whether an array is C-ordered.

exercises.title: Which element is mine?
exercises.statement:
A launch creates a grid of blocks, and each block holds the same number of threads. Every thread runs the same function and has to work out which element it is responsible for.

Write two functions.

  • global_index(t) returns the position of thread t in a one-dimensional launch: its block number times the number of threads in a block, plus its own number inside the block. Use t.blockIdx.x, t.blockDim.x and t.threadIdx.x.
  • blocks_needed(n, block_size) returns the smallest number of blocks of block_size threads that gives each of n elements a thread of its own.

For the blocks: divide and round up. With whole numbers that is (n + block_size - 1) // block_size.

These two lines open almost every CUDA program. In CUDA C they read:

int blocks = (n + blockSize - 1) / blockSize;

Rounding up means the last block usually has threads with no element to work on. The next exercise deals with them.

from collections import namedtuple

Dim = namedtuple("Dim", "x y")

The launch rounds the number of threads up to whole blocks, so there may be more threads than elements. A thread whose index is n or more must do nothing.

A kernel returns nothing. Its result is what it writes into y.

exercises.statement:
Write the kernel blur(t, n, src, dst). For an element with a neighbour on each side, dst[i] becomes the mean of src[i - 1], src[i] and src[i + 1]. The first and the last element are copied unchanged. Threads past the end do nothing.

exercises.statement:
A thousand threads cannot all add into one variable: each reads the old total, adds its value and writes back, and most of the additions are lost. A sum is built in rounds instead.

In the round with stride s, the thread at index i adds data[i + s] into data[i], but only when i is a multiple of 2 * s and i + s < n. After the rounds with stride 1, 2, 4 and so on, the total is in data[0].

Then write the host function gpu_sum(values, block_size). It copies values, calls launch(reduce_step, (blocks, 1), (block_size, 1), n, stride, data) once per round while the stride is less than n, and returns the total. It returns 0 for an empty list and leaves values as it was.

d = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
launch(reduce_step, (2, 1), (4, 1), 5, 1, d)
print(d)
launch(reduce_step, (2, 1), (4, 1), 5, 2, d)
print(d)
launch(reduce_step, (2, 1), (4, 1), 5, 4, d)
print(d)

v = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]
print(gpu_sum(v, 4), gpu_sum(list(range(1, 14)), 4), gpu_sum([], 4), gpu_sum([5], 4), v)

seen = []
_launch = launch


def launch(kernel, grid, block, *args):
    seen.append(args[1])
    _launch(kernel, grid, block, *args)


print(gpu_sum(list(range(100)), 16), seen)

hints: The kernel is three lines: the index, one condition with two parts, one addition.
if i % (2 * stride) == 0 and i + stride < n: then data[i] += data[i + stride].
The host: data = list(values), stride = 1, then while stride < n: launch and double the stride. Return data[0], after handling the empty list.
exercises.explanation:
In CUDA C the kernel is:

__global__ void reduce_step(int n, int stride, float *data) {
    int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    if (i % (2 * stride) == 0 && i + stride < n) data[i] += data[i + stride];
}

A hundred numbers take 7 rounds instead of 99 additions in a row: the depth is log n. No two threads touch the same element in a round, because the thread at i reads i + stride, and i + stride is never a multiple of 2 * stride, so no thread writes it. That is why the shuffled order cannot change the answer.

Real code does the rounds inside each block with shared memory and one launch, or calls atomicAdd, or uses a library. The idea of pairing up in a tree is the same in all of them, and it is how MPI_Reduce and an OpenMP reduction clause work as well.
exercises.given:
import random
from collections import namedtuple

Dim = namedtuple("Dim", "x y")
Thread = namedtuple("Thread", "blockIdx threadIdx blockDim gridDim")


def launch(kernel, grid, block, *args):
    """Run kernel once for every thread, in a shuffled order.

    In CUDA C this is kernel<<<grid, block>>>(args).
    grid is (blocks in x, blocks in y).
    block is (threads in x, threads in y).
    A GPU promises no order, so neither does this.
    """
    grid, block = Dim(*grid), Dim(*block)
    ids = [(bx, by, tx, ty)
           for by in range(grid.y) for bx in range(grid.x)
           for ty in range(block.y) for tx in range(block.x)]
    random.Random(len(ids)).shuffle(ids)
    for bx, by, tx, ty in ids:
        t = Thread(Dim(bx, by), Dim(tx, ty), block, grid)
        kernel(t, *args)

exercises.title: Running totals in log n rounds
exercises.statement:
The running totals of [3, 1, 4, 1] are [3, 4, 8, 9]. On one processor that is a loop that carries a total, which looks impossible to share out. It can be done in rounds.

In the round with offset k, every element becomes itself plus the element k places to its left, if there is one:

  • dst[i] = src[i] + src[i - k] when i >= k
  • dst[i] = src[i] otherwise

Offsets double each round: 1, 2, 4, and so on while the offset is less than n. Every thread reads the values from before the round, so a round reads one list and writes another.

Write the kernel scan_step(t, n, offset, src, dst) and the host function gpu_running_totals(values, block_size), which launches launch(scan_step, (blocks, 1), (block_size, 1), n, offset, a, b) once per round and returns the running totals as a new list.

tests.test:

dst = [None] * 5
launch(scan_step, (2, 1), (4, 1), 5, 1, src, dst)
print(dst, src)
out = [None] * 5
launch(scan_step, (2, 1), (4, 1), 5, 2, dst, out)
print(out)

v = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6]
print(gpu_running_totals(v, 3), gpu_running_totals([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 4), gpu_running_totals([], 4), gpu_running_totals([7], 4), v)

seen = []
_launch = launch


def launch(kernel, grid, block, *args):
    seen.append(args[1])
    _launch(kernel, grid, block, *args)


print(gpu_running_totals([1] * 20, 8), seen)

hints: The kernel: index, bounds check, then one of two assignments depending on whether i >= offset.
The host is the blur's host again: two lists, launch, swap. Only the stopping rule differs: while offset < n, doubling the offset.
After round 1 each element holds a sum of 2 neighbours, after round 2 a sum of 4, then 8. When the reach passes the start of the list the element is finished.
exercises.explanation:
In CUDA C the kernel is:

__global__ void scan_step(int n, int offset, const float *src, float *dst) {
    int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    if (i >= n) return;
    dst[i] = (i >= offset) ? src[i] + src[i - offset] : src[i];
}

This is the Hillis and Steele scan. It finishes in log n rounds but does about n log n additions in total, more than the n − 1 of the simple loop: it buys speed with extra work. The PRAM model in your syllabus is where that trade is measured, as time against total work. Scans turn up wherever threads need to know where to write: compacting an array, building a histogram, sorting.
