exercises.title: Word count
exercises.statement:
A MapReduce job is two functions.

  • mapper(record) looks at one record and returns a list of (key, value) pairs.
  • reducer(key, values) gets one key with the list of all the values that were paired with it, and returns one result.

The framework does the rest: it spreads the records over workers, gathers the pairs by key, and calls the reducer once per key.

Write mapper(line) and reducer(word, counts) so that the job counts how often each word appears. A word is whatever split() gives, in lower case. The mapper returns (word, 1) for every word in the line. The reducer returns (word, total).

tests.test:
lines = ['the cat sat', 'The dog sat', 'the end', '']
print(map_reduce(lines, mapper, reducer))

lines = ['a b a', 'b a', 'a a a c', 'c b', 'a']
print(map_reduce(lines, mapper, reducer, combiner=lambda word, counts: [reducer(word, counts)]))

hints: The mapper does not count anything. It only says: here is this word, once.
[(word, 1) for word in line.lower().split()].
The reducer adds the values up: (word, sum(counts)). Counting how many values there are would be wrong as soon as a worker has added some of them together already.
exercises.explanation: The third test puts the reducer to work as a combiner: each worker adds up its own pairs before sending them on, so ('a', 1) five times travels as ('a', 5) once. That only works because the reducer sums the values. One that returned len(counts) would pass the second test and fail the third. A combiner is safe when the operation gives the same answer however the values are grouped, which is true of sums, minimums and maximums.

exercises.title: A mean that survives a combiner
exercises.statement:
The records are (sensor, reading) pairs. The job must return each sensor's mean reading as (sensor, mean).

Each worker runs the combiner on the readings it happens to hold, so one sensor's readings reach the reducer already combined in uneven groups. A mean of those groups' means would be wrong. Carry a sum and a count instead.

Write three functions.

  • mapper(record) returns [(sensor, (reading, 1))].
  • combiner(sensor, values) gets a list of (sum, count) pairs and returns [(sensor, (total sum, total count))].
  • reducer(sensor, values) gets a list of (sum, count) pairs and returns (sensor, mean).

tests.test:
records = [('a', 1), ('a', 2), ('a', 6), ('b', 10), ('b', 20), ('a', 3)]
print(map_reduce(records, mapper, reducer, combiner), map_reduce(records, mapper, reducer))

records = [('t', v) for v in [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 100]] + [('u', 7)]
print(map_reduce(records, mapper, reducer, combiner, workers=4))

hints: The value that travels is a pair. The mapper makes the smallest such pair: one reading, counted once.
The combiner and the reducer both start the same way: add up the first parts, add up the second parts.
total = sum(s for s, c in values), count = sum(c for s, c in values). The combiner returns [(sensor, (total, count))]; the reducer returns (sensor, total / count).
exercises.explanation: The mean of [0, 0, 100] is 33.3, but the mean of the means of [0, 0] and [100] is 50. A mean cannot be combined piece by piece; a sum and a count can. Federated averaging has exactly this shape: each client sends its update together with the number of samples behind it, and the server divides once at the end. Weighting clients by sample count is the combiner done properly.

exercises.title: Who sends to whom in a tree sum
exercises.statement:
p processes, ranked 0 to p - 1, each hold one number. They want the total at rank 0. If every process sent straight to rank 0, rank 0 would receive p - 1 messages one after another. A tree does it in about log p rounds.

In the round with step s, starting at 1 and doubling, every rank r that is an odd multiple of s sends what it holds to rank r - s, which adds it to its own. A rank that has sent takes no further part.

Write reduce_rounds(p). It returns a list with one entry per round; each entry is the list of (sender, receiver) pairs of that round, in ascending order of sender. Stop when only rank 0 still holds a value.

tests.test:
r = reduce_rounds(1000)
print(len(r), sum(len(x) for x in r), r[-1])

hints: In round 1 the senders are 1, 3, 5, ... In round 2 they are 2, 6, 10, ... What is the gap between senders in the round with step s?
The senders of a round are s, 3s, 5s, ...: range(s, p, 2 * s). Each sends to itself minus s.
rounds = [], s = 1, then while s < p: append [(r, r - s) for r in range(s, p, 2 * s)] and double s.
exercises.solution:
def reduce_rounds(p):
    rounds = []
    s = 1
    while s < p:
        rounds.append([(r, r - s) for r in range(s, p, 2 * s)])
        s *= 2
    return rounds
exercises.explanation: A thousand processes need 999 messages either way, but the tree spreads them over 10 rounds in which many pairs talk at once. This is what MPI_Reduce does inside, and it is the same pairing as the GPU sum: stride there, step here. In an MPI program each rank runs the same code and decides from its own rank and the step whether to call MPI_Send or MPI_Recv in this round.

exercises.title: Bisection
exercises.statement:
f is a continuous function, and f(lo) and f(hi) have opposite signs, so f is zero somewhere between them.

Write bisect_root(f, lo, hi, tol). Repeat while hi - lo is greater than tol: take the midpoint; if f is exactly zero there, return it; otherwise keep the half in which the sign still changes. At the end return the midpoint of what is left.
exercises.starter:
def bisect_root(f, lo, hi, tol):
    pass

tests.test:
import math
print(round(bisect_root(lambda x: math.cos(x) - x, 0, 1, 1e-7), 5), round(bisect_root(lambda x: 3 - x, 0, 10, 1e-7), 5))

calls = []
def f(x):
    calls.append(x)
    return x ** 3 - 5
root = bisect_root(f, 0, 4, 0.01)
print(round(root, 2), len(calls) < 25, bisect_root(lambda x: x - 2, 0, 4, 1e-9))

hints: Compare the sign at the midpoint with the sign at lo. If they are the same, the root is in the upper half.
Two values have the same sign when their product is positive. Evaluate f(lo) once and keep it.
mid = (lo + hi) / 2, fm = f(mid). If fm == 0 return mid. If f_lo * fm > 0: lo, f_lo = mid, fm; else hi = mid. After the loop return (lo + hi) / 2.
exercises.explanation: Each step halves the interval, so the error after k steps is at most the starting width divided by 2ᵏ. That is slow, one binary digit per step, but it cannot fail: the root never leaves the bracket. It is binary search on a continuous function, and the same idea as the binary search exercises under DSA.

exercises.title: Newton's method
exercises.statement:
Newton's method improves a guess x for a root of f by following the tangent line at x down to zero: the new guess is x - f(x) / df(x), where df is the derivative of f.

Write newton(f, df, x0, steps). Start from x0, apply the update steps times, and return the result.
exercises.starter:
def newton(f, df, x0, steps):
    pass

tests.test:
f = lambda x: x * x - 2
df = lambda x: 2 * x
print([round(newton(f, df, 1.0, k), 6) for k in range(5)])
print(round(newton(lambda x: x ** 3 - 27, lambda x: 3 * x * x, 2.0, 8), 6), newton(lambda x: 2 * x - 6, lambda x: 2, 100.0, 1))

import math
print(round(newton(lambda x: math.cos(x) - x, lambda x: -math.sin(x) - 1, 1.0, 5), 6))

hints: It is a loop that runs steps times and changes one variable.
Inside the loop: x = x - f(x) / df(x).
With steps equal to 0 the loop does not run and the function returns x0 itself.
exercises.explanation: Look at the first test: 1.5, then 1.4167, then 1.414216. The number of correct digits roughly doubles each step, which is called quadratic convergence. Bisection needs about 23 steps for the accuracy Newton reaches in 4. The price is that Newton needs the derivative and a starting guess near the root: where the derivative is close to zero the tangent is nearly flat and the next guess flies far away. The secant method replaces df with the slope between the last two guesses.

exercises.title: Slopes from function values
exercises.statement:
When only the values of f are available, a slope has to be estimated from them.

Write two functions.

  • forward_diff(f, x, h) returns (f(x + h) - f(x)) / h.
  • central_diff(f, x, h) returns (f(x + h) - f(x - h)) / (2 * h).

tests.test:
f = lambda x: x ** 3
print(round(forward_diff(f, 2, 0.01), 4), round(central_diff(f, 2, 0.01), 4))

import math
print(round(central_diff(math.sin, 0, 0.1), 5), round(forward_diff(math.sin, 0, 0.1), 5), central_diff(lambda x: 5 * x + 1, 3, 0.5))

f = lambda x: x * x
print([round(abs(forward_diff(f, 1, h) - 2), 6) for h in (0.1, 0.01)], [round(abs(central_diff(lambda x: x ** 3, 1, h) - 3), 6) for h in (0.1, 0.01)])

hints: Both are one line each. They are the slope of a straight line through two points on the curve.
Forward uses the points at x and x + h. Central uses x - h and x + h, which are 2 * h apart.
Mind the brackets in the denominator: / (2 * h), not / 2 * h.
exercises.explanation: The last test is the lesson. Making h ten times smaller makes the forward error ten times smaller, and the central error a hundred times smaller: forward is first order, central is second order. The central difference is what a gradient check uses in Stage 1 of the build, to confirm a hand-derived gradient. h cannot shrink for ever: below about 1e-8 for the forward form, rounding in f(x + h) - f(x) grows faster than the formula's own error falls.

exercises.title: The trapezoidal rule
exercises.statement:
To estimate the area under f between a and b, cut the interval into n strips of equal width h and treat each strip as a trapezoid. Added up, that is

h * (f(x0) / 2 + f(x1) + f(x2) + ... + f(x_{n-1}) + f(xn) / 2)

where x0 = a, xn = b and the points are h apart.

Write trapezoid(f, a, b, n).
exercises.starter:
def trapezoid(f, a, b, n):
    pass

tests.test: print(trapezoid(lambda x: x * x, 0, 1, 4), trapezoid(lambda x: 2 * x + 1, 0, 3, 1))

f = lambda x: x * x
print([round(abs(trapezoid(f, 0, 3, n) - 9), 6) for n in (10, 20, 40)])

hints: h = (b - a) / n. The points are a + i * h for i from 0 to n.
The two end values count half, every value in between counts in full.
total = (f(a) + f(b)) / 2, then add f(a + i * h) for i in range(1, n), then return h * total.
exercises.explanation: The last test doubles the strips twice, and the error falls by four each time: 0.045, 0.01125, 0.0028. The error is proportional to h², second order. Romberg integration uses exactly that regularity: it combines the results for n and 2n so that the h² terms cancel. The rule is also the standard first MPI program: each process integrates its own slice of the interval and the slices are added with MPI_Reduce.

exercises.title: Simpson's rule
exercises.statement:
Simpson's rule fits a parabola through each pair of strips instead of a straight line through each strip. With n strips of width h, where n is even:

h / 3 * (f(x0) + 4 * f(x1) + 2 * f(x2) + 4 * f(x3) + ... + 4 * f(x_{n-1}) + f(xn))

The inner points take the weights 4, 2, 4, 2, ..., 4: 4 at odd positions, 2 at even ones.

Write simpson(f, a, b, n). n is always even.
exercises.starter:
def simpson(f, a, b, n):
    pass

tests.test: print(round(simpson(lambda x: x ** 3, 0, 2, 2), 6), round(simpson(lambda x: x ** 4, 0, 1, 4), 6))

f = lambda x: x ** 4
print([round(abs(simpson(f, 0, 2, n) - 6.4) * 1e4, 3) for n in (4, 8, 16)])

hints: h = (b - a) / n. Start the total with the two end values.
Loop i from 1 to n - 1. The weight is 4 when i is odd and 2 when it is even.
total += (4 if i % 2 else 2) * f(a + i * h), and at the end return h / 3 * total.
exercises.explanation: The first test integrates x³ exactly with two strips, although a parabola cannot follow a cubic: the errors on the two sides cancel. Simpson's rule is exact for polynomials up to degree 3 and its error is proportional to h⁴, so doubling the strips divides the error by 16, as the last test shows. Ten strips give sin to four decimal places where the trapezoidal rule needed a hundred for three.

exercises.title: The polynomial through given points
exercises.statement:
Through n points with different x values there is exactly one polynomial of degree at most n - 1. Lagrange's form writes it without solving any equations:

P(x) = sum over i of ys[i] * L_i(x)

where L_i(x) is the product, over every j other than i, of (x - xs[j]) / (xs[i] - xs[j]). Each L_i is 1 at xs[i] and 0 at every other given point.

Write lagrange(xs, ys, x). It returns the value of that polynomial at x.

tests.test:
import math
xs = [0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2]
print(round(lagrange(xs, [math.sin(v) for v in xs], 0.75), 4), round(math.sin(0.75), 4), round(lagrange([-1, 0, 1], [1, 0, 1], 3), 6))

hints: Two nested loops: the outer one adds the terms, the inner one builds one L_i as a running product.
Start each product at 1 and skip j == i, otherwise you divide by zero.
For each i: term = ys[i]; for each j != i: term *= (x - xs[j]) / (xs[i] - xs[j]); then total += term.
exercises.explanation: Five points of the sine curve reproduce sin(0.75) to three or four decimal places. The last value is the warning: outside the range of the points the polynomial follows its own shape, not the function's. With many equally spaced points the polynomial also swings wildly near the ends of the range, which is Runge's phenomenon; that is the reason for splines, which join low-degree pieces, and for Chebyshev points, which crowd toward the ends.

exercises.title: Back substitution
exercises.statement:
U is an upper triangular matrix, given as a list of rows: everything below the diagonal is zero, and nothing on the diagonal is. The last equation of U x = b therefore has one unknown, the one before it has two, and so on.

Write back_substitute(U, b). It returns the solution x as a list.
hints: Work from the last row up. When you reach row i, every x[j] with j > i is already known.
Row i says U[i][i] * x[i] + (the sum of U[i][j] * x[j] for j > i) = b[i].
for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1): compute s as that sum, then x[i] = (b[i] - s) / U[i][i].
exercises.explanation: This costs about n²/2 multiplications, against n³/3 for the elimination that produces the triangle. That gap is why LU factorisation pays: factor once, then each new right-hand side costs only two cheap triangular solves.

exercises.title: Gaussian elimination with pivoting
exercises.statement:
Write solve(A, b). A is a square matrix as a list of rows and b a list. Return the solution of A x = b as a list. Do not change A or b.

Use elimination with partial pivoting. For each column k in turn:

  1. Among rows k and below, find the one whose entry in column k is largest in absolute value, and swap it into row k.
  2. Subtract a multiple of row k from each row below it, chosen so that the row's entry in column k becomes zero. Do the same to b.

What is left is upper triangular. Finish with back substitution.

tests.test: print([round(v, 6) for v in solve([[2, 1], [1, 3]], [3, 5])], [round(v, 6) for v in solve([[0, 2], [1, 1]], [4, 3])])
print([round(v, 4) for v in solve([[1e-12, 1], [1, 1]], [1, 2])], [round(v, 6) for v in solve([[4]], [2])])

hints: Copy first: M = [row[:] for row in A] and y = b[:], then work on the copies.
The pivot row: p = max(range(k, n), key=lambda r: abs(M[r][k])). Swap rows k and p in both M and y.
For each row r below k: factor = M[r][k] / M[k][k]; subtract factor * M[k][c] from M[r][c] for every column c from k, and factor * y[k] from y[r]. Then back substitution on M and y.
exercises.solution:
def solve(A, b):
    n = len(b)
    M = [row[:] for row in A]
    y = b[:]
    for k in range(n):
        p = max(range(k, n), key=lambda r: abs(M[r][k]))
        M[k], M[p] = M[p], M[k]
        y[k], y[p] = y[p], y[k]
        for r in range(k + 1, n):
            factor = M[r][k] / M[k][k]
            for c in range(k, n):
                M[r][c] -= factor * M[k][c]
            y[r] -= factor * y[k]
    x = [0.0] * n
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        s = sum(M[i][j] * x[j] for j in range(i + 1, n))
        x[i] = (y[i] - s) / M[i][i]
    return x
exercises.explanation: The second system in the first test has a zero in the top-left corner, so elimination without a swap divides by zero. The last test is the subtler case: a pivot of 1e-12 is not zero, but dividing by it produces numbers so large that the other entries are rounded away, and the answer comes out as [0, 1]. Swapping the largest entry into the pivot position keeps every multiplier at most 1, which keeps the rounding under control.

exercises.title: LU factorisation
exercises.statement:
Write lu(A). A is a square matrix as a list of rows. Return two matrices (L, U) with L times U equal to A, where U is upper triangular and L is lower triangular with ones on its diagonal.

This is elimination with its multipliers kept. To clear column k of row r you subtract factor = U[r][k] / U[k][k] times row k. Store that factor in L[r][k]. Do not swap rows; the tests never need it. Do not change A.

tests.test:
A = [[4, -2, 1], [-2, 4, -2], [1, -2, 4]]
L, U = lu(A)
P = [[round(sum(L[i][k] * U[k][j] for k in range(3)), 9) for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)]
print(P == A, [round(U[i][i], 4) for i in range(3)], L[0][1], U[2][0])

hints: Start with U as a copy of A with float entries, and L as the identity matrix.
The loops are the elimination loops: for each column k, for each row r below it.
factor = U[r][k] / U[k][k]; L[r][k] = factor; then U[r][c] -= factor * U[k][c] for every column c from k on.
exercises.explanation: Solving A x = b now takes two triangular solves: L y = b forwards, then U x = y backwards. The n³ work is done once, however many right-hand sides follow. The determinant comes free as the product of U's diagonal. A real library swaps rows as in the exercise before and returns the swaps too, as P A = L U. For a symmetric positive definite matrix the same idea gives the Cholesky factor, with half the work.

exercises.title: Jacobi iteration
exercises.statement:
For a large system, elimination can cost too much. An iterative method starts from a guess and improves it.

Jacobi's method solves equation i for x[i], using the previous guess for all the other unknowns:

new_x[i] = (b[i] - sum of A[i][j] * x[j] for j != i) / A[i][i]

Write jacobi(A, b, steps). Start from all zeros, do steps sweeps, and return the guess. Every value in a sweep is computed from the guess of the sweep before.

tests.test:
A = [[4, 1], [2, 3]]
b = [1, 2]
print([round(v, 4) for v in jacobi(A, b, 1)], [round(v, 4) for v in jacobi(A, b, 2)], jacobi(A, b, 0))

hints: Keep two lists: x, the previous guess, and new_x, the one being built. Replace x only when the sweep is complete.
For each i, add up A[i][j] * x[j] over every j except i.
new_x = [(b[i] - sum(A[i][j] * x[j] for j in range(n) if j != i)) / A[i][i] for i in range(n)], then x = new_x.
exercises.explanation: Because each new value depends only on the previous sweep, all n updates of a sweep can run at once. Jacobi is the blur kernel again: two buffers, one launch per sweep. It converges when each diagonal entry outweighs the rest of its row, which is called diagonal dominance. The systems that come from heat flow and other differential equations have that property and are mostly zeros, which is where iterative methods beat elimination.

exercises.title: Gauss-Seidel iteration
exercises.statement:
Gauss-Seidel changes one thing in Jacobi's method: as soon as a new x[i] is computed it is used, in the same sweep, for the unknowns after it. There is one list, updated in place.

Write gauss_seidel(A, b, tol). Start from all zeros. After each sweep, look at the largest absolute change that any x[i] made in that sweep; stop when it is below tol. Return (x, sweeps): the solution and the number of sweeps done, counting the last one.

tests.test:
x, sweeps = gauss_seidel([[4, 1], [2, 3]], [1, 2], 1e-6)
print([round(v, 5) for v in x], sweeps)

A = [[10, -1, 2], [-1, 11, -1], [2, -1, 10]]
x, sweeps = gauss_seidel(A, [6, 25, -11], 1e-8)
print([round(v, 5) for v in x], sweeps)

hints: One list x. Inside a sweep, the sum for row i reads x[j] straight from that list, so it picks up the values already updated.
Track the largest change of the sweep: change = max(change, abs(new - x[i])) before you store new.
while True: do a sweep, add 1 to sweeps, and if change < tol: return x, sweeps.
exercises.explanation: Using the newest values roughly halves the number of sweeps Jacobi needs on these systems. The cost is that the sweep is now a chain: x[1] waits for x[0], so it cannot be shared out as it stands. Parallel versions colour the unknowns like a chessboard and update all of one colour at once. Successive over-relaxation, SOR, goes one step further: it moves each unknown past its Gauss-Seidel value by a factor ω between 1 and 2, x[i] += ω * (new - x[i]), and with a good ω converges far faster.

exercises.title: A chain after n steps
exercises.statement:
A Markov chain has states 0 to n - 1 and a transition matrix P, given as a list of rows: P[i][j] is the probability of moving to state j when in state i. Each row adds up to 1.

start[i] is the probability of beginning in state i. After one step, the probability of being in state j is the sum over i of start[i] * P[i][j].

Write after_steps(P, start, steps). It returns the list of probabilities after that many steps.

tests.test:
P = [[0.9, 0.1], [0.5, 0.5]]
print([round(v, 4) for v in after_steps(P, [1, 0], 1)], [round(v, 4) for v in after_steps(P, [1, 0], 2)], after_steps(P, [1, 0], 0))

P = [[0.9, 0.1], [0.5, 0.5]]
print([round(v, 4) for v in after_steps(P, [1, 0], 50)], [round(v, 4) for v in after_steps(P, [0, 1], 50)])

hints: One step is a new list of the same length. Entry j collects probability from every state i.
new[j] = sum(dist[i] * P[i][j] for i in range(n)).
Repeat that steps times, replacing dist with new each time, and return dist.
exercises.explanation: The distribution is a row vector multiplied by P on its right, once per step. The Chapman-Kolmogorov equations say the same thing for matrices: the n-step probabilities are the entries of P multiplied by itself n times. The last test starts in two different states and ends in the same place after 50 steps. The chain has forgotten where it began; the next exercise finds that limit directly.

exercises.title: The stationary distribution
exercises.statement:
A distribution pi is stationary for a chain when one more step leaves it unchanged: pi times P is pi again. For a chain that can get from every state to every other, and is not periodic, every start drifts toward it.

Write stationary(P, tol). Start from the even distribution, 1 / n in every state. Keep taking one step; stop when no entry changed by more than tol in the last step, and return the distribution.
hints: It is the step from the exercise before inside a while True: loop.
After computing new, measure max(abs(new[j] - dist[j]) for j in range(n)).
Replace dist with new first, then return it if that largest change is at most tol.
exercises.explanation: This is power iteration: multiply by the matrix until the vector stops moving. What it finds is the left eigenvector of P for eigenvalue 1. The second test is a birth and death chain, the kind behind queueing models, and its answer [0.25, 0.5, 0.25] can be checked by hand from the balance of flow between neighbours: 0.25 × 0.5 going up from state 0 equals 0.5 × 0.25 coming down from state 1. How fast the iteration settles is set by the second largest eigenvalue, which is the mixing time question from your data science course.

exercises.title: A single-server queue
exercises.statement:
Customers arrive at random at an average rate of lam per hour, and one server handles them at an average rate of mu per hour. This is the M/M/1 queue. When lam < mu it settles into a steady state with:

  • utilisation rho = lam / mu, the fraction of time the server is busy
  • L = rho / (1 - rho), the mean number in the system
  • Lq = rho * rho / (1 - rho), the mean number waiting, not counting the one being served
  • W = 1 / (mu - lam), the mean time in the system
  • Wq = rho / (mu - lam), the mean time spent waiting

Write mm1(lam, mu). It returns a dictionary with the keys "rho", "L", "Lq", "W" and "Wq". If lam is not less than mu the queue grows without limit: return None.

tests.test: print({k: round(v, 4) for k, v in mm1(2, 3).items()})
print({k: round(v, 4) for k, v in mm1(9, 10).items()}, mm1(3, 3), mm1(5, 4))

hints: Check the unstable case first and return None.
Compute rho once and use it in the other formulas.
Build the dictionary with the five keys spelled exactly as in the statement.
exercises.explanation: The last test is why this model matters outside an exam. A server that can handle 10 requests an hour answers in 12 minutes at half load, an hour at 90%, and ten hours at 99%. Delay does not rise in proportion to load; it explodes as utilisation nears 1. That is the reason a model server is sized to run well below full use. The formulas obey Little's law, L = lam * W, which holds for any queue in steady state, not only this one.

exercises.title: PageRank
exercises.statement:
links[i] is the list of pages that page i links to. Pages are numbered 0 to n - 1.

A surfer on page i follows one of its links, chosen evenly, with probability d. Otherwise the surfer jumps to one of the n pages chosen evenly. A page with no links at all always jumps to a page chosen evenly.

Write pagerank(links, d, steps). Start with rank 1 / n on every page and apply this update steps times:

new[j] = (1 - d) / n + d * (sum of rank[i] / len(links[i]) over the pages i that link to j) + d * (total rank of the pages with no links) / n

Return the list of ranks.

tests.test:
r = pagerank([[1, 2], [2], [0]], 0.85, 60)
print([round(v, 4) for v in r], round(sum(r), 6))

r = pagerank([[1], []], 0.85, 80)
print([round(v, 4) for v in r], round(sum(r), 6), pagerank([[1], [0]], 0.5, 0))

hints: Each update builds a new list. Start every entry at (1 - d) / n plus the share from the pages without links, which is the same for every page.
Then push rank along the links: for each page i with links, each page j it links to receives d * rank[i] / len(links[i]).
dangling = sum(rank[i] for i in range(n) if not links[i]); new = [(1 - d) / n + d * dangling / n] * n; then the loop over links adds to new[j].
exercises.explanation: PageRank is the stationary distribution of a random walk on the web graph, found by the power iteration of the exercise before. The random jump is what makes the chain able to reach every state, so that a single stationary distribution exists. Pushing rank along the links, instead of building an n by n matrix, is a sparse matrix-vector product: the work is proportional to the number of links. It is also the textbook MapReduce job, with one map and one reduce per update.

exercises.title: The best-fit direction
exercises.statement:
The rows of A are points in space. The direction along which they spread the most is the first right singular vector of A: the unit vector v that makes the length of A v as large as possible. That largest length is the first singular value.

Power iteration finds it. Start with v as the vector of all ones, scaled to length 1. Then repeat steps times: compute w = A v, then u = Aᵀ w (multiply by A, then by its transpose), and replace v with u scaled to length 1.

Write top_singular(A, steps). A is a list of rows. Return (sigma, v): the length of A v for the final v, and that v as a list.

tests.test:
s, v = top_singular([[3, 0], [0, 1]], 30)
print(round(s, 4), [round(x, 4) for x in v])

s, v = top_singular([[1, 1], [1, 1]], 5)
print(round(s, 4), [round(x, 4) for x in v])
s, v = top_singular([[2, 0], [1, 1], [0, 2]], 40)
print(round(s, 4), [round(x, 4) for x in v])

pts = [[1, 2], [2, 4.1], [3, 5.9], [4, 8.2], [-1, -2.1]]
s, v = top_singular(pts, 60)
print(round(s, 3), [round(x, 3) for x in v], round(v[1] / v[0], 2))

hints: Write two helpers first: the length of a vector, and a matrix times a vector.
w[i] = sum(A[i][j] * v[j] for j) has one entry per row. u[j] = sum(A[i][j] * w[i] for i) has one entry per column.
After the loop compute w = A v once more and return (length of w, v).
exercises.explanation:
The last test has five points near the line y = 2x, and the direction found has slope 2.03. That is the best-fit line through the origin in the sense of the singular value decomposition: it minimises the perpendicular distances, where least squares regression minimises the vertical ones.

v is the eigenvector of AᵀA with the largest eigenvalue, and that eigenvalue is sigma squared, which is the link between the SVD and the eigen-decomposition. Subtract the centre of the points first and this is the first principal component of PCA.
